taxa.note: Pink gills that darken to chocolate, a brown spore print, and no sac at the base. Each of those alone separates it from a destroying angel, which keeps white gills, drops a white print, and stands in a bag. East of the Rocky Mountains this name covers a group of look-alike grassland species (A. andrewii, A. porphyrocephalus var. pallidus, A. argenteus and others) that only spores or DNA tell apart; true A. campestris is not confirmed here.

lookalikes.note: Scratch the very base of the stem and cut it open. A yellow-stainer goes chrome yellow there within seconds and smells of ink or phenol; a field mushroom does neither and has only a thin, quickly collapsing ring. Old yellow-stainers can lose both the staining and the smell.

A destroying angel keeps white gills at every age, drops a white print, and sits in a membranous sac. If the base was not dug up, that question is not answered. Smell does not settle it: both can smell of nothing.

taxa.note: The bulb at the base is usually abrupt and rimmed, and split vertically as though cleft with a knife, though not every collection shows it. lookalikes.note: A destroying angel is white throughout, never stains, and its cap is usually bare. This is grey to brown with scattered warts and browns where handled. Both can have a bulb, so dig up the base: a loose white sac around it means destroying angel.

The false death cap is pale greenish yellow fading to whitish. Its cut flesh does not change, though the cap and stem sometimes stain purplish to brownish. This is grey to brown and stains reddish brown where handled, most of all near the base. Both have a rimmed bulb that can be split, both can be sticky, and both may smell faintly of raw potato, so none of those settles it.

taxa.note: An abruptly bulbous base with a rim or gutter, a pale greenish-yellow cap that fades quickly to near white, and sometimes a faint smell of raw potato. The eastern North American mushroom under this name is not the European species: Kuo calls it A. citrina f. lavendula, Tulloss A. lavendula with two look-alikes.

lookalikes.note: Both have an abrupt rimmed bulb that can be split, and both can smell of raw potato. The cleft-foot browns on the stem and bulb when handled and has a grey-brown to whitish cap; this one is pale greenish yellow fading to white.

An old false death cap fades nearly white and can pass for a destroying angel. The angel has a bald cap and a loose, free sac at the base; the false death cap usually carries soft patches, and its volva clings tight to a rimmed bulb. Dig the base out.

The false death cap is pale yellow to white with soft patches on the cap. The death cap is usually olive to greenish, though some are yellowish or brownish, and its cap is usually bare. Both can have a swollen base and smell does not settle it, so dig up the base: a loose white sac around it means death cap. Any doubt, treat it as the death cap.

lookalikes.note: Both have yellow warts, a yellow to orange cap and a bulb, and both cap edges can be lined. The fly agaric is usually bigger, with a shaggy stem and rings of scales at the top of the bulb. Flavoconia has a bald or slightly roughened stem and loose yellow powder at the base.

taxa.note: A red-orange cap with a deeply lined margin, yellow gills, a yellow-orange skirtlike ring, and a large white sac at the base. All of them together, or leave it. The sac and the ring separate it from Amanita parcivolvata, which has neither. The sac, the yellow gills and the bald cap separate it from the warted fly agarics (A. persicina, A. muscaria var. guessowii), whose bulbs carry scales and no bag. It can also be confused with A. phalloides (Wikipedia). Sources: Kuo 2024, mushroomexpert.com/amanita_jacksonii.html; Tulloss, amanitaceae.org/?Amanita+jacksonii.

unrecorded.taste: No raw taste recorded. Tulloss: 'Odor not discernible. Taste not recorded.' Kuo and Wikipedia give none. Web results only describe cooked flavour on culinary blogs, which is not the field taste test.

lookalikes.note: The yellow-orange fly agaric is toxic. It has white gills, a warted cap and a bulb ringed with shaggy veil bands, never a white bag. A. jacksonii has yellow gills, a bald cap and a tall sac.

The peach-orange fly agaric is toxic. It has white to faintly pink gills, yellowish warts and a bulb with scattered veil patches, not a sac, and it grows under pines and hemlock. A. jacksonii has yellow gills, a bald cap and a tall white sac.
Amanita parcivolvata has no ring and no sac, only loose powdery volval bits at the base, and its cap usually carries scattered warts. Gill colour will not separate them: both are yellowish.

lookalikes.note: The American Caesar has a yellow-orange skirt ring, a tall white sac and a bald cap. Rain can wash this one's warts off, so check the ring and dig out the base.

The yellow-orange fly agaric is stockier, with more prominent warts, a skirt ring and concentric shaggy veil rings on its bulb, and a whitish, somewhat shaggy stem. This one has no ring and a pale yellow, dusty-powdery stem, and grows under oaks, often in grass.

The peach fly agaric's fragile ring is often lost, and both grow with oak and pine, so neither the ring nor the tree reliably separates them. Look at the stem: pale yellow and dusted with yellow powder in this one, whitish and somewhat shaggy or fibrillose in persicina. Also look at the gills (cream to pale yellow here, white to faintly pink in persicina) and the bulb, which is larger in persicina.

hazard.note: Presumed to produce the pantherine (ibotenic acid / muscimol) syndrome, as in the rest of the muscaria group: delirium and sedation rather than organ damage. Rarely fatal, reliably unpleasant.
hazard.source: Tulloss, amanitaceae.org/?Amanita+persicina; North American Mycological Association poisoning references

taxa.note: This region's fly agaric: peach to melon-orange rather than scarlet, often fading to nearly cream at the margin, with pale yellowish warts that wash off in rain. The base is a bulb carrying scattered yellowish veil patches, only rarely in neat rings, and never a bag. The lack of a bag is what separates the group from the deadly white ones. The ring is fragile and often gone.

unrecorded.bruising_speed: No published description found that records it (audit of September 2026).
unrecorded.koh: Neither Kuo nor Tulloss gives a KOH reaction. Tulloss's macrochemical tests are paracresol and syringaldazine only.

season.note: A long season with a heavy peak in October.

lookalikes.note: No field character in the schema reliably separates them, and both are toxic in the same way. Guessowii is lemon to egg-yolk yellow, usually has well-defined concentric veil rings on the bulb and a more persistent ring. Persicina is peach to melon with only scattered bulb patches. Caps overlap in orange and the line between them is geography as much as colour.

taxa.note: A sac at the base and no ring at all, with a deeply lined cap edge. lookalikes.note: A destroying angel in its egg stage is a white ball in the soil, and cut in half it shows the outline of a cap and gills inside. This grows on wood and is uniform paste throughout. Cut every one.

The common earthball is a hard, thick-skinned, scaly yellowish ball on soil or moss, rarely on wood. Cut it: its inside is grey to purple-black from early on, never uniform white like the stump puffball's. Some earthballs cause serious poisoning.
The gem-studded puffball grows on the ground and has conical spines that leave round scars when they fall. The pear-shaped puffball is on wood, is only finely spiny, and has white cords at its base.

lookalikes.note: The shaggy scalycap is covered in coarse recurved scales on both cap and stem, and drops a brown print. The honey mushroom drops white.
The red-banded webcap has rusty bands around the stem rather than a membranous ring, a cobwebby veil when young, and a rust-brown print.

The deadly Galerina grows on the same wood, sometimes side by side with honey mushrooms. It is smaller, with rusty-brown gills, a thin ring or ring zone, and a rust-brown print. The honey mushroom has whitish gills, a white print and a sturdy yellow-edged ring. Take a print from every cluster.

The jack-o'-lantern also grows in clusters at the base of hardwoods and on buried roots. It is orange all through, gills and flesh included, and has no ring. The honey mushroom has whitish gills, white flesh and a ring.
The ringless honey mushroom looks much the same, in the same tight clusters, but has no ring or ring zone at all. It usually fruits a few weeks earlier.

taxa.note: Small, grey-brown, with a sharp navel at the centre of the cap and gills running down the stem. On rotting wood and moss.

hazard.note: A hard crust on old wood. Nothing documented against it.
hazard.source: North American Mycological Association poisoning references

taxa.note: A hard pale crust on long-dead bare oak, cracked into small tiles with dark lines between them, like crazed glaze. It is stuck fast and does not peel; the tiles are the whole identification.

unrecorded.bruising: Neither source says. Its family (Stereaceae) includes species that bleed red when cut (Stereum sanguinolentum, S. rugosum), so 'no' cannot be recorded as structural.
unrecorded.koh: No KOH reaction is published; the sources give only the spores' amyloid reaction.

season.note: Recorded here in every month: it persists rather than fruits and passes.

lookalikes.note: The parchments make thin brackets with a free edge. This is flat against the wood and cracked into tiles.
